In a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll, voters said they favored Democrats over Republicans on the generic congressional ballot by 5 percentage points. They disapproved of Trump’s job performance by a 25-point margin and his handling of the economy by even more.

For Democrats, the strategy for the midterms is simple: speak to the mounting economic frustrations of voters, including those who took a chance on Trump in 2024 but now feel betrayed.

To anchor it in reality, recent polls of the generic congressional ballot show Democrats leading by 6–8 points.

The good news for Republicans is that the bottom probably won’t fall out any further. For Democrats to reach 54 seats or beyond, they would need to hunt in Florida (Baseline: R+10) or South Carolina (R+15), which are both currently occupied by Republican appointees. [...] Finally, there’s Texas. With an R+11 Baseline, it’s the most Republican-leaning 2026 Senate battleground — but it’s become increasingly competitive. (In 2018, when Democrat Beto O’Rourke came within 3 points of unseating GOP Sen. Ted Cruz, Texas’ Baseline was R+14.5.)
